transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-07
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42m
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Cygnus Head of ML), Aisha Khan (Infra Lead), Tom Rivera (Security)

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Discovery focused on latency and throughput requirements for Cygnus Retail's recommender and chat assistants.
- Key concerns: p95 latency targets for streaming and non-streaming, concurrent active sessions (1k+), token/sec benchmarking, data residency and KMS integration, SOC2 + SSO.
- Next steps: send benchmarks, schedule POC scoping, exchange security docs.

Topics: latency SLAs, concurrency, streaming vs batch, token/sec benchmarks, dedicated vs hosted, security/compliance

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, um i'm jordan from redwood, i'll kick us off - priya's our solutions engineer, she'll dig into the latency/throughput stuff.
[00:18] Marcus: hey jordan thanks, marcus here, head of ml at cygnus. quick high level: we run a recommendations API and a customer chat experience, both need <200ms p95 ideally for the recommender, chat can tolerate up to 500ms but streaming is important for UX.
[00:33] Jordan: got it, so two workloads — recommender is low-latency high-qps, chat is streaming with partials. that matches a lot of customers. what are your concurrency numbers?
[00:45] Aisha: right now peak concurrent sessions hit about 800 active streams across regions, but during promo windows it spikes to ~1.6k. average token/sec per session is around 12-18 tokens/sec for chat, recommender calls are short 20-60 tokens each but at very high rps.
[01:05] Priya: okay that's helpful. are your models in-house or are you using public models via a provider? and are you considering quantized variants for cost?
[01:14] Marcus: we have a mix. some custom fine-tuned 7b variants hosted on-prem; we're exploring hosted inference for scale and dedicated reserved capacity for predictable latency. quantization is on the roadmap but quality needs validation.
[01:29] Tom: security is a big deal — we need SOC2 audit evidence, SAML SSO, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integration. if private deployment is needed we might look at VPC peering or on-prem package.
[01:45] Jordan: totally, we support SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and KMS integrations. private and VPC options exist for regulated traffic. we'll share the security packet after this call.
[01:56] Marcus: thanks. for the recommender p95 target — you said sub-200ms is feasible. is that on hosted or dedicated? and what's the concurrency influence?
[02:08] Priya: good question. sub-200ms p95 for short prompts at low seq lengths typically requires dedicated capacity or a high-tier hosted instance with warm workers. the main factors are model size, quantization, batch size, and KV cache hits. with dedicated pools we can pin reserved GPUs and guarantee warm KV cache and lower tail latency.
[02:29] Marcus: how do you handle KV cache across concurrent requests? we have a lot of shared prefixes in recommender prompts.
[02:35] Priya: we do prefix/KV caching and dynamic routing. if you have high prefix reuse, the effective per-token time drops because the KV cache avoids recomputing early layers. that helps p95 heavily. we'll want sample prompts to estimate cache hit rates.
[02:49] Aisha: i'll send prompt sets and a 30-day histogram.
[02:52] Jordan: awesome. another question: streaming — do you support chunked partial outputs with low first-byte latency? that's critical for our chat UX.
[03:03] Priya: yes, we support streaming with partial tokens and also function/tool calling. streaming first-byte is often network+model startup bound. with dedicated warm workers and continuous batching tuned for small latencies we can hit 100-200ms first-byte for many setups, but it depends on tokenization and model compute.
[03:23] Marcus: what's token/sec throughput we should expect for a single GPU? we need to model cost for 1k concurrent streams.
[03:31] Priya: rough numbers: on a modern A100/RTX-class equivalent, for a 7B non-quantized model you might see ~200-500 tokens/sec depending on optimizations; with int8 quantization you can increase tokens/sec 1.5-2x, and on larger models tokens/sec drops. but this is very workload-specific. for 1k concurrent streams at 12 tokens/sec each that's 12k tokens/sec sustained — you'd want a pool of GPUs with good batching and maybe autoscale.
[04:00] Aisha: that's helpful. do you provide tools to simulate that throughput or do we need to run our own bench?
[04:07] Jordan: we have a benchmark harness we can share and also run tests as part of a POC. usually we exchange sample prompts and a traffic profile, we run a token/sec/p95 sweep and share a spreadsheet with latency percentiles vs concurrency.
[04:20] Marcus: perfect. what about network egress and rate limiting? during spikes we need graceful degradation and fallback to smaller models.
[04:29] Priya: smart routing and model variants are part of the offering — you can configure policies to route to lower-cost model variants or dedicated fallback capacity. autoscaling and burst capacity help too; the tradeoff is cost vs p95.
[04:43] Tom: from a security perspective, how do you isolate customer data in dedicated pools? encryption-at-rest? audit logs?
[04:49] Jordan: dedicated pools get tenant isolation at the worker and network layer. we support encrypted volumes, KMS key-managed encryption, and audit logging surfaced in the console with token-level traces. we'll include the architecture diagram in the pack.
[05:02] Aisha: do you support customer-managed keys (BYOK) for KMS?
[05:07] Jordan: yes, BYOK/HSM integrations are supported in Private deployments and available for Dedicated via integrations. we'll add that to the doc.
[05:15] Marcus: ok let's dig more into latency math — for recommender at 20-60 tokens, how much does batching hurt p95 at high qps?
[05:24] Priya: batching is a double-edged sword. it increases throughput and reduces cost per token but can add latency because we wait to fill batches. for short requests you can use smaller batch sizes or continuous batching tuned to a latency SLO. we also have adaptive batching that tightens batch windows when p95 grows. but for strict 200ms p95 at high concurrency dedicated warm workers with small batch targets are usually the way to go.
[05:46] Marcus: curious about our worst-case — spike to 1.6k concurrent, recommender tight 200ms — what's fallback?
[05:54] Priya: you can set multi-tier routing: primary dedicated pool, fallback to a high-priority hosted pool or a cheaper quantized variant with lower compute. Redwood can automatically route when queueing risk exceeds threshold. for spikes we'd recommend pre-warmed burst capacity and multi-region routing to reduce tails.
[06:14] Jordan: do you have SLA constraints or contract windows for reserved capacity? Aisha?
[06:20] Aisha: we'd want a monthly committed capacity with the option to burst; SLA ideally 99.9% p95 within region during business hours. cost is sensitive — especially if we pay for idle GPUs. can you describe autoscale billing?
[06:34] Priya: Dedicated allows committed baseline with burst-on-demand; billing can be structured to a monthly commit plus metered burst. autoscaling policy examples: keep N warm workers, autoscale up when queue > threshold. we can share sample pricing scenarios.
[06:48] Marcus: about model variants — if we want to use a fine-tuned 7B on-prem and Redwood hosted for peaks, is there a path to hybrid?
[06:58] Jordan: yes, hybrid routing is a core pattern — you can keep a private deployment for sensitive traffic and route non-sensitive or burst traffic to Redwood Hosted or Dedicated pools. we maintain consistent API and rollout controls across environments.
[07:11] Aisha: great. for the POC we'd want benchmarks for both streaming chat and short recommender calls. can you handle both in one test plan?
[07:19] Priya: absolutely. typical POC has two phases: (1) Controlled throughput sweep for short requests measuring p50/p95/p99 at increasing concurrency and (2) streaming scenario measuring first-byte latency and tail for partial tokens and end-to-end token/sec. we'll instrument KV cache hit assumptions too.
[07:36] Marcus: what's the timeline to get those results?
[07:39] Jordan: once we have prompts and traffic profile, initial bench can be done in 5-7 business days; a deeper multi-region run may take 10-14 days.
[07:48] Tom: will your benchmark include quality checks when quantized variants are used? we can't degrade recommendation quality beyond an internal threshold.
[07:56] Priya: yes, we pair latency benches with evals — small eval suites comparing outputs, embedding similarity, and business-metric proxies. we'll include that in the test plan.
[08:10] Marcus: pricing and cost modeling — we need estimates of $/1M tokens at our expected mix and cost for reserved vs burst.
[08:18] Jordan: we'll run a model: recommended pool sizes, projected tokens/sec, and cost scenarios for hosted vs dedicated vs private. I'll include $/token and effective $/concurrent-session curves in the spreadsheet.
[08:31] Aisha: a few infra details: we use Cloud provider X across two regions, have strict egress rules and bastion-only access. we need VPC peering or private link and firewall rules before any hosted connectivity.
[08:44] Jordan: understood — we support VPC peering and private link options; for security we can use mTLS and IP allowlists. we'll collect firewall ports needed for the POC.
[08:55] Tom: and audit logs need to be forwarded into our SIEM — can you stream logs?
[09:00] Priya: yes, audit logs and traces can be exported to S3, a logging endpoint, or forwarded to common SIEMs. we'll include the log format and retention options.
[09:10] Marcus: let's talk model size — if we move to an 13B model for chat, how do tails change?
[09:17] Priya: larger models increase per-token compute and latency; tokens/sec will drop. p95 tails get wider unless you use more GPUs or quantize. sometimes for chat we use mixed models: smaller LMs for intent/short responses and a larger model for complex queries triggered selectively.
[09:33] Marcus: for our numbers — 1k concurrent streams, avg 14 tokens/sec -> 14k tokens/sec. assuming an optimized 7B at 350 tokens/sec per GPU, that's ~40 GPUs sustained. is that math reasonable?
[09:46] Priya: yes that's the right ballpark ignoring batching gains. with batching you can improve tokens/sec per GPU; also KV cache hits for recommender reduce compute. we'll model both conservative and optimistic scenarios.
[09:58] Aisha: how do warm workers work? what's the cost of keeping N workers warm for immediate low-latency responses?
[10:04] Jordan: warm workers are reserved instances with model loaded and KV cache warmed; cost is unit GPU-hour. we can recommend a baseline number to meet p95 targets and autoscale policies for spikes. the spreadsheet will show cost vs latency curves for different warm pool sizes.
[10:20] Marcus: are network latencies included? our app server to redwood region RTT is ~30-50ms. we need total p95 including network.
[10:28] Priya: we'll measure from client e2e to get realistic p95; network RTT is additive so regional placement matters. multi-region routing can keep RTT low.
[10:36] Jordan: quick note — we commonly report p50/p95/p99 for server-side processing and provide an e2e estimate if you give us RTT.
[10:45] Marcus: can you show an example benchmark output in the spreadsheet?
[10:49] Jordan: yes, sample sheet will include latencies (p50/p95/p99), CPU/GPU utilization, tokens/sec, cost per hour, and notes on cache hit assumptions.
[10:58] Aisha: about the POC infra — do you need us to open ports or create a service account?
[11:04] Priya: for hosted tests we typically set up a service account with scoped API keys and optional VPC peering for private link tests. we'll provide step-by-step.
[11:13] Marcus: let's cover failure modes — what happens if a worker fails under load?
[11:19] Priya: we have worker-level health checks, retries, and queueing. active sessions may be retried or routed to fallback pools. we also replicate sessions across capacity tiers where possible to limit visible disruptions.
[11:34] Marcus: anything tricky about streaming reconnects? we need idempotency and partial state recovery.
[11:39] Priya: streaming clients should support resume semantics; we typically use a short-lived token and a session ID to recover or continue partial outputs. we'll add recommended client patterns.
[11:51] Tom: regulatory question — if we store logs for 90 days, can you guarantee deletion on request?
[11:57] Jordan: yes, we support retention policies and deletion workflows; for Private deployments you can configure local retention and full data ejection on termination.
[12:07] Marcus: ok good. let's talk about evaluation thresholds for quantized models — do you have typical quality deltas for int8 on recomms?
[12:15] Priya: qualitatively int8 often has small accuracy deltas but it's model and task dependent. we'll include a short eval comparing sample outputs and embedding cosine deltas. you can set a business-metric threshold (e.g., CTR delta < 1%) to qualify quantized variants.
[12:31] Aisha: on telemetry, we want per-request token-level cost and latency breakdowns; is that available?
[12:38] Jordan: yes console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and traces. we can also stream raw metrics to your monitoring stack.
[12:47] Marcus: for next steps let's capture what we need to start the POC.
[12:51] Jordan: list is: sample prompts for recommender and chat, 30-day traffic histogram, desired p95 targets and budget, decision stakeholders and legal contact for security docs.
[13:03] Marcus: i'll share prompts and traffic. legal will want to review SOC2 and DPA.
[13:09] Jordan: we'll send SOC2 and DPA, plus the benchmark spreadsheet.
[13:14] Aisha: can you also include a sample firewall/VPC config?
[13:18] Priya: yes we'll include ports, IP ranges, and private link setup steps.
[13:23] Marcus: any limitations on model upload or fine-tuning in Dedicated/Private?
[13:29] Jordan: Private allows full control for model upload and fine-tuning on-prem. Dedicated supports custom model mounting with vetted images; there are security review steps. we'll sync on process during POC scoping.
[13:41] Tom: how long to onboard a new private deployment if needed?
[13:45] Priya: on-prem/private deployments can take 4-8 weeks depending on network approvals and provisioning; VPC-based private control plane is faster, usually 2-4 weeks.
[13:56] Marcus: ok great. pricing again — please include examples for 40 GPUs and 80 GPUs so we can run budgets.
[14:03] Jordan: will do.
[14:05] (longer section)
[14:10] Priya: a couple of technical clarifications — when you say 12-18 tokens/sec per stream is that measured after sampling or does that include client-side post processing?
[14:18] Marcus: that's measured server-side as average token output; client-side processing negligible.
[14:22] Priya: okay that helps. for the recommender prompts, can you confirm typical sequence lengths?
[14:27] Marcus: most are 20-60 tokens; spikes to 120 in some cases.
[14:32] Priya: great, that'll keep costs manageable.
[14:35] Jordan: quick commercial note — we can do a time-boxed POC with a small committed amount of dedicated capacity and apply credits toward committed purchase if you sign.
[14:45] Marcus: good to know.
[14:47] Aisha: any red flags you see from our described constraints?
[14:51] Priya: nothing we can't handle; main risk is quality regression with aggressive quantization — we'll validate that. capacity spikes are addressable with burst and routing. network egress rules will require minor configuration.
[15:04] Marcus: alright let's summarize next steps then.
[15:07] Jordan: i'll send the benchmark spreadsheet, pricing scenarios, SOC2 + DPA, and firewall/VPC guide by 6/9. priya will draft the POC test plan by 6/11. you'll send prompts and traffic by 6/8.
[15:20] Marcus: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[15:24] Tom: one last question — do you have any references for retail customers you can share?
[15:28] Jordan: yes we'll share 1-2 anonymized case studies and a reference contact if needed.
[15:33] Marcus: perfect. thanks, talk soon.

[41:58] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up in email and set the scoping call. bye.
